texts.error.arcade_ram_no_memory: There is not enough memory for the board's RAM.
texts.error.arcade_ram_too_large: The board cannot carry that much RAM.
texts.error.card_off: The save data carries a card for slot %1 (%2), but there is no card in slot %3: switch the Memory Card %4 setting on.
texts.error.guncon_control: The GunCon 2 in port %1 has no control called "%2". This core's controls are keyed by the names the emulated gun declares, and that one is gone: the upstream version this core builds changed it.
texts.error.iop_module: "%1" is an IOP module (.irx). Those are drivers a program loads while it runs (a memory card driver, a pad driver), not something the machine can be started on. Give it the program instead: a disc image, or the .elf that would have loaded this.
texts.error.media_missing: The game's media is not where the project said it was.
texts.error.media_unreadable: The board's drive cannot read this image.
texts.error.no_boot_program: This machine is a NAMCO board, and the project has no boot program in it.
texts.error.no_media: This machine is a NAMCO board, and the project has no game media in it.
texts.error.no_such_patch: The project turns on the patch "%1", which PCSX2's patch collection in this core does not have for this game (%2, checksum %3). Turn it off in the project's settings.
texts.error.no_vulkan_bridge: The renderer setting is vulkan-hw, and no Vulkan was handed over (this computer may have no Vulkan driver, or this Chimera is older than its Vulkan bridge).
texts.error.save_name: This machine does not read save data called "%1". It reads memory cards (.ps2 files: memcard1.ps2 and memcard2.ps2, the names Export Save Data writes, PCSX2's own Mcd001.ps2 and Mcd002.ps2, or a card under any other name, which goes in slot 1 and then slot 2) and bios.nvm.
texts.error.three_cards: The save data carries more memory cards than the console's two slots (%1, %2 and %3). Keep two.
texts.error.truncated_dump: This disc image is a damaged dump (its sectors are cut short). A clean dump of this disc is needed.
texts.error.two_cards: The save data carries two cards for slot %1, %2 and %3. Keep one.
texts.firmware.bios_bin.about: OpenPS2BIOS 0.2, an open replacement for the console's BIOS, written for emulators. It holds no Sony code, and anyone may download it and pass it on (MIT licence). The file is OpenPS2BIOS-0.2.bin, from https://github.com/TamaribaEmu/OpenPS2BIOS/releases/tag/v0.2. It is new and does less than a console's own BIOS: it starts discs but not a program file on its own, and it does not read a memory card back yet, so a game may not start, and a save may not load. This core was tested on it with its own test program, not with games. A different version is a different machine.
texts.firmware.bios_bin.about_2: The arcade board's own boot ROM, copied from a COH-H motherboard. This is NOT a retail PlayStation 2 BIOS, and a retail one does not work: the arcade boot software differs in many module interfaces, and an arcade game does not start on it. A COH-H ROM identifies itself in its ROMVER text (region T followed by a Z). The board it came from is identified by its EXTINFO build serial, which is the only thing that tells the three boards apart. This project asks for the System 246 Rack C ROM, serial 20021119-163841, 2 MB. Redump calls the file ps2-arcade-0100tz-20021119-163841.bin. MAME has the same bytes as r27v1602f.7d in its sys246 BIOS set, and the file is also found as 246C.bin.
texts.firmware.bios_bin.about_3: The arcade board's own boot ROM, copied from a COH-H motherboard. This is NOT a retail PlayStation 2 BIOS, and a retail one does not work: the arcade boot software differs in many module interfaces, and an arcade game does not start on it. A COH-H ROM identifies itself in its ROMVER text (region T followed by a Z). The board it came from is identified by its EXTINFO build serial, which is the only thing that tells the three boards apart. This project asks for the System 256 ROM, serial 20040519-145634, 2 MB. Redump calls the file ps2-arcade-0100tz-20040519-145634.bin, and MAME has the same bytes as r27v1602f.8g in its sys256 BIOS set. A Super System 256 runs this same ROM with a faster bus clock, which is why both machines ask for it.
texts.firmware.bios_bin.about_4: The arcade board's own boot ROM, copied from a COH-H motherboard. This is NOT a retail PlayStation 2 BIOS, and a retail one does not work: the arcade boot software differs in many module interfaces, and an arcade game does not start on it. A COH-H ROM identifies itself in its ROMVER text (region T followed by a Z). The board it came from is identified by its EXTINFO build serial, which is the only thing that tells the three boards apart. This project asks for the System 256 ROM as a 4 MB file with its two megabytes written twice. A copying tool that reads the whole address range produces this, and the file is widely found under the name 256.BIN. It describes the same System 256 machine as the 2 MB file above. The bytes are different, and this core accepts firmware only by its exact hash.
texts.firmware.bios_bin.about_5: The arcade board's own boot ROM, copied from a COH-H motherboard. This is NOT a retail PlayStation 2 BIOS, and a retail one does not work: the arcade boot software differs in many module interfaces, and an arcade game does not start on it. A COH-H ROM identifies itself in its ROMVER text (region T followed by a Z). The board it came from is identified by its EXTINFO build serial, which is the only thing that tells the three boards apart. This project asks for the ROM of the COH-H A-000-010 board, serial 20000901-114731, 4 MB, usually called COH-H31000.BIN. It is the earliest of the three and the one the arcade development boards had.
texts.firmware.bios_bin.label: OpenPS2BIOS 0.2
texts.firmware.bios_devkit.about: The BIOS of a development kit (DEVKIT) or debug station, copied from a PlayStation 2 development unit. It starts like a retail BIOS and tells a game that it is a development machine, which some games check. This project asks for %1. The file is usually called %2. Another copy of the same version is accepted. A different version is a different machine, and you choose it with the Boot ROM setting.
texts.firmware.bios_dvd.about: The firmware of the DVD PLAYER. It is not a boot ROM, and a machine does not start from it. It is listed only for completeness. If the machine does not start, this is the reason. This project asks for %1. The file is usually called %2. Another copy of the same version is accepted. A different version is a different machine, and you choose it with the Boot ROM setting.
texts.firmware.bios_retail.about: The console's own BIOS, copied from a PlayStation 2 you own. This project asks for %1. The file is usually called %2. Another copy of the same version is accepted. A different version is a different machine, and you choose it with the Boot ROM setting.
texts.game_setting.patch_about: From PCSX2's patch collection. It changes the game's own code, so a movie made with it plays back only with it.
texts.setting.arcade_game.about: NAMCO's part number for this game: "NM" and five digits, such as NM00004 for Tekken 4, NM00007 for Soul Calibur II and NM00019 for Tekken 5. It identifies the game the way a MAME set name does. The JVS board (the cabinet's input board) reads it to know how this cabinet's control panel was wired: which switch is which button, whether there is a wheel, a drum or a pair of levers, and where a light gun's sensor reports. A project that leaves it empty gets the board's general wiring. That starts and can be played, but it is not the cabinet the game was made for.
texts.setting.arcade_media.about: The kind of medium the game was supplied on. It decides how the board's own disk controller (ATA/ATAPI) reads it. A COH-H board has no disc drive of its own, so the media is in the NAMCO board's drive and not in the console's tray. The exception is a CD game, which also asks the console for the disc, so this core puts it in both places. You choose the kind here, and it is not guessed. The PCSX2 version that this board support comes from looks it up in a game database, but a project states its own settings.
texts.setting.arcade_panel.about: How the cabinet's JVS input wiring is laid out. 'derived' takes it from the Game ID. That is right for every game the board knows, and a project should normally leave it there. The other choices force a layout, for a game that is not in the table or a cabinet that somebody converted. The choice decides which of the Arcade Panel's controls the board actually reads. A fighting cabinet reads six switches and no analog controls, a racing cabinet reads the wheel and the pedals, and a Taiko cabinet reads eight drum sensors. It is part of the machine, so a movie records it. The panel's controls are named after the WIRING and not after any game. 'P1 Button 1' is the first switch on player one's panel, and what it does depends on the game: a punch in one game, a gear change in another. Every control has a default key, so a cabinet can be played as soon as it starts, and you find out what each control does by playing the game. Nothing here is set up for a particular game.
texts.setting.arcade_ram.about: How much memory the cabinet has on the NAMCO board, in megabytes. A System 246 Rack A takes expansion boards of 32 or 64 MB in two slots. Racks B and C have 64 MB built in. Wangan Midnight's cabinet has 128. A System 256 has none, and should be set to 0. It is a setting, and is not guessed from the game, for two reasons. The board's memory is part of every savestate this core makes, and 128 MB of it takes space. And a cabinet is something a person built, so a project has to be able to say what it has. A game that reads memory the cabinet does not have reads zeros, as it would from an empty expansion slot.
texts.setting.arcade_region.about: The regional signature that a System 256 reads from the board's own iLink id. The Taiko Drum Master games use it to decide which region they are in. 'none' leaves the id that the machine's BIOS has. It does nothing on a System 246.
texts.setting.bios.about: WHICH PlayStation 2 this project is. A PS2 cannot run a single instruction without its BIOS, and the emulator has no built-in replacement for it. The BIOS decides the console's region, its language, its menus, and what a game checks when it refuses to run. Each choice expects one exact file. The firmware page names the file and the SHA-1 it must have. Two projects with different BIOS versions are different machines and cannot share movies. The retail consoles are listed first. After them come the ROMs of the development kits (DEVKIT) and debug stations. After them comes the DVD PLAYER firmware, which is the ROM of the disc player and not a boot ROM, so a machine does not start from it. Last is OpenPS2BIOS, an open replacement written for emulators: it holds no Sony code and anyone may download it, but it does less than a console's own BIOS, so a game may not run on it.
texts.setting.bios.about_2: WHICH arcade board this project is, in the only way the hardware can be told apart. Sony never changed the version or the date in a COH-H ROM: every one says v1.00 (2000-03-06). So the EXTINFO build serial inside the file is what tells them apart, and it names the board. 20021119-163841 is a System 246 Rack C. 20040519-145634 is a System 256 (the Super 256 runs the same ROM with a faster bus clock). 20000901-114731 is the COH-H A-000-010 development board. 'coh-h-256-mirrored' is the same System 256 ROM as a 4 MB file with its two megabytes written twice, which some copying tools produce. It is offered because that file is in circulation, and this core accepts firmware only by its exact hash. A RETAIL PlayStation 2 BIOS does not work and is not offered here. The arcade boot software differs in many module interfaces, and an arcade game does not run on a retail BIOS. The firmware page names the file and the SHA-1 it must have.
texts.setting.cpu_core.about: Which processor implementations run the machine. The recompilers translate the code of the EE, the IOP and both VUs to x86 code as it runs. This is how PCSX2 itself normally plays, and it is several times faster. The interpreters execute every instruction one at a time, which is the slowest and most literal way. They are DIFFERENT MACHINES, because the recompiler's EE floating point does not give the same results as the interpreter's. So the project and the movie record the choice, and a movie made with one does not play back with the other.
texts.setting.deinterlace.about: How the console's two fields become one picture, when the game produces fields at all. In an interlaced mode a PS2 sends out HALF a picture per frame: 224 lines of 448, with the other half in the next frame. Something has to decide what a single field looks like as a whole frame. But many games draw WHOLE frames instead, and running one of those through a deinterlacer destroys half of it: the picture then always has one row from this frame and one row from the previous frame. 'auto' asks the machine which of the two it is doing. It leaves a whole frame alone and rebuilds a field picture with 'adaptive'. This is what PCSX2 itself does, and it should normally be left on. The other choices force one method. 'adaptive' compares this field with the three before it and decides for each pixel whether to keep a line or to make one from the lines above and below. Still pictures keep their full detail, and moving ones show no comb pattern. 'weave' puts each field's lines back in their proper places. That is the full picture the television showed, and fast motion shows a comb pattern, as it does on the real machine. 'weave-bff' and 'adaptive-bff' are the same with the order of the fields swapped, for a game that looks one line out of place. 'blend' is weave with the comb pattern softened. 'bob' shows the current field alone, scaled up. It never shows a comb pattern, and it has half the vertical detail. 'off' hands over the field stretched and places nothing, which makes a still screen move up two lines and back down on every frame.
texts.setting.dip_monitor_sync.about: The third DIP switch. It says which sync frequency the cabinet's monitor uses, 15 kHz or 31 kHz. It is reported to the game, and some games read it to choose a video mode.
texts.setting.dip_test.about: The test switch of the input/output board, as on the real board. It is a DIP SWITCH, which is why it is a setting and not a column in the movie. (The cabinet's TEST BUTTON is a separate control, Test in the Arcade Panel, and the board reports the two in one bit.) When the switch is on, the cabinet starts into its own test menu and not into the game. The coin settings, the input test and the game's own options are there. The position of the switch is part of the machine a movie was recorded on.
texts.setting.dip_video_sync_split.about: The fourth DIP switch. It says whether the cabinet's monitor takes composite sync or separate horizontal and vertical sync. It is reported to the game as part of the same status.
texts.setting.dip_video_voltage.about: The second of the input/output board's four DIP switches. It is reported to the game as part of the board's status. Like the other three it is part of the machine, so a movie records it. The default is the position a cabinet has when it leaves the factory.
texts.setting.dithering.about: PCSX2's dithering choice, the same as its Settings > Graphics > Rendering > Dithering. The console's graphics chip (the GS) can dither a picture it draws in 16-bit colour, which hides colour banding behind a fine pattern of dots. 'unscaled', the default and PCSX2's, dithers the way the console does, with dots one console pixel wide at any internal resolution. 'scaled' makes the dots larger as the internal resolution goes up, which looks more like the console on a big screen; at 1x it is the same as 'unscaled'. 'off' does not dither: flat bands of colour instead of dots. 'force32' draws every 16-bit picture as if it were 32-bit, which removes both the dots and the banding and usually gives the cleanest picture. It applies to the OpenGL and Vulkan renderers only. The software renderer dithers exactly as the console does and ignores this. THIS SETTING CAN AFFECT WHETHER A MOVIE PLAYS BACK, in the same way as Texture Filtering: it decides what the graphics card puts into the surfaces it draws, and a game that reads its own picture back reads those bytes. The project records it, and a movie made with one value needs the same value to play back.
texts.setting.fast_boot.about: Starts the disc's own program directly, without the console's start-up sequence. The BIOS animation takes about twenty seconds of emulated time, and the machine is in a different state at the end of it. So this is part of what a movie was recorded on, and not only a convenience: a movie made with it does not play back without it.
texts.setting.fxaa.about: PCSX2's own fast approximate anti-aliasing (FXAA). It is a shader that runs over the finished picture, after the console's display circuits have combined it. It applies to the OpenGL and Vulkan renderers only. The software renderer has no shader stage, so there it stays off whatever is chosen here. Nothing reads the finished picture back, so this cannot change the machine. When measured on Maximo, Gran Turismo 4 and Street Fighter EX3 it changed the picture and not one byte of memory, the audio or the lag count. It is a project setting because that is the only way a value reaches a core, and because it is how the movie's picture looked. A movie made with it plays back without it, and the other way round. Changing it restarts the core, as changing any setting does.
texts.setting.internalresolution.about: PCSX2's own upscaling. Every surface is drawn at this multiple of the console's size, so 3D looks sharper and a video can be made at a higher resolution. It applies to the OpenGL and Vulkan renderers only. The software renderer draws at the console's own size and ignores this. It works best with 'opengl-hw', because an OpenGL without a graphics card pays for every extra pixel on the processor. THIS SETTING CAN AFFECT WHETHER A MOVIE PLAYS BACK, in the same way as Texture Filtering. A game that reads its own picture back gets it through PCSX2's texture cache, which scales an upscaled surface back down, and the result is not always byte for byte the picture at the console's size. The project records it, and a movie made with one value needs the same value to play back. 2D games gain little, and some show seams at 2x and above, as they do in PCSX2.
texts.setting.machine.about: Which of this package's machines the project is. 'ps2' is the PlayStation 2 console. The other three are NAMCO's arcade boards. These ARE PlayStation 2s: a Sony COH-H motherboard with a NAMCO board in the expansion bay. They need a different kind of project. It has an arcade BIOS from a COH-H board and not a retail one, the game's security dongle, its media and a boot program, each as a file of its own kind, and it has a JVS control panel in place of the controller ports. 'system246' runs the main processor (the EE) at the console's 294.912 MHz. 'system256' runs it a third faster (393.216 MHz) and 'system256super' a half faster (442.368 MHz). The clock speed is the difference between those two boards, and a game recorded on one does not play back on the other. The machine decides the whole project: its inputs, its files, its settings and its firmware. A movie made on one machine does not run on another.
texts.setting.memcard1.about: Whether there is a memory card in the console's slot 1. Games check on their first screen and behave differently without one, so it is part of the machine. The card's contents are save data. A card to start from goes in the project's Save Data as memcard1.ps2, and Emulator > Export Save Data writes it out under the same name.

texts.setting.multitap1.about: Whether a multitap is plugged into port 1. A multitap turns the port's one socket into four. A game can SEE the multitap whether or not anything is plugged into it, and controllers 3 to 5 and their memory cards can be reached only through it. That is why it is a setting of its own and is not worked out from the controllers. Otherwise a memory card in a slot would depend on a controller being in that slot.
texts.setting.multitap2.about: Whether a multitap is plugged into port 2. A multitap turns the port's one socket into four. A game can SEE the multitap whether or not anything is plugged into it, and controllers 6 to 8 and their memory cards can be reached only through it. That is why it is a setting of its own and is not worked out from the controllers. Otherwise a memory card in a slot would depend on a controller being in that slot.
texts.setting.port1.about:
What is plugged into port 1. 'dualshock2' is the standard controller, which almost all games expect. The special controllers are for the games made for them. 'guitar' is the Guitar Hero controller (a strum bar, five frets, a whammy bar and a tilt sensor). 'jogcon' is Ridge Racer's dial with force feedback. 'negcon' is Namco's twisting pad. 'popn' is the nine buttons of Pop'n Music. They are offered only on the two ports of the console itself.

'guncon2' is Namco's light gun, for Time Crisis and the dozen or so games like it. It is not a controller. It plugs into the console's USB socket with this same number, so choosing it leaves the CONTROLLER socket empty, as on a real console with a light gun. The number matters as well as the choice, because a few games look for the gun only on USB port 2. The place the gun points at is stored in the movie as two ordinary axes, so a recording plays back anywhere. The mouse is not read.

It is part of the machine. A game asks what is connected, so two projects that differ here are different machines and cannot share movies.

texts.setting.renderer.about: Which renderer draws the picture. 'software' is PCSX2's own software renderer and the default. It runs completely inside the core on the processor, so the picture is the same on every computer that plays the movie and does not depend on your graphics driver. Two runs of 2401 frames of Gran Turismo 4 with it are identical byte for byte at frames 900, 1500 and 2400. 'opengl' is PCSX2's OpenGL renderer, the one PCSX2's developers test with and most games are checked with. Here it draws with an OpenGL that is built into the core (Mesa's softpipe). It also gives the same picture on every computer, and it is slower than the software renderer. 'opengl-hw' is the same OpenGL renderer drawing on your computer's graphics card. It and 'vulkan-hw' are the fastest where there is a graphics card: the same 2401 frames took 9.6 seconds on a GTX 1060, against 20.6 seconds with the software renderer. It does NOT give the same picture everywhere. The picture comes from a driver that is outside the core and outside the savestate, and it differs between computers. A movie recorded with it records that a graphics card drew the picture. It is not the default because it is the choice that has gone wrong in use. The picture of a run that was recorded again could come back visibly wrong (ToolAssisted-run/chimera issues 55 and 56). And when a build or a computer cannot give it OpenGL, it falls back to the softpipe, which on Windows crashes after about a thousand frames. 'vulkan-hw' is PCSX2's Vulkan renderer drawing on your computer's graphics card. What is said of 'opengl-hw' is true of it: the picture comes from a driver outside the core, it differs between computers, and a movie recorded with it records that a graphics card drew the picture. On a GTX 1060 it is as fast as 'opengl-hw': 3700 frames of Street Fighter EX3 took 13.6 seconds with it and 13.8 seconds with 'opengl-hw', and the last picture was the same. It has nothing to fall back on. It needs a graphics driver that has Vulkan and a Chimera that hands Vulkan to cores, and without either the project does not start and says why. No renderer changes the machine: the console's main memory after 2401 frames is identical with the software renderer and with the graphics card. So the choice is about the picture and the speed, and never about the run.

texts.setting.rtc_month.about: The month on the console's clock.
texts.setting.rtc_second.about: The second on the console's clock.
texts.setting.rtc_year.about: The year on the console's clock. A PS2 has a clock with a battery. Without this setting PCSX2 would read your computer's clock, and then every run would be a different machine: some games take their random numbers from the clock, and every save is stamped with it. The default is 2020, which is late enough for every PS2 game to accept it as today's date.
texts.setting.texturefiltering.about: How a texture is sampled when one texture pixel does not land on exactly one screen pixel. It applies to the OpenGL and Vulkan renderers only. The software renderer samples the way the console's graphics chip (the GS) does and ignores this. 'machine' is what the game asked the GS for, texture by texture, and gives the picture the console drew. 'nearest' always takes the nearest texture pixel. 'linear' always blends, which smooths a game that asked for nearest. 'linearNoSprites' does the same but leaves sprites alone, which keeps 2D text sharp. THIS SETTING CAN AFFECT WHETHER A MOVIE PLAYS BACK. It decides what the graphics card puts into every surface it draws, and PCSX2 writes such a surface back into the console's memory whenever a game reads its own picture. For such a game, the bytes it reads depend on this value. When measured on Maximo and Gran Turismo 4 (up to 6000 frames) it changed the picture and not one byte of memory. The project records it all the same, and a movie made with one value needs the same value to play back. Choose it when the project is created.
texts.setting.verbose.about: Makes PCSX2 report what it is doing on the standard error output: which BIOS and disc it found, what the input/output processor (the IOP) loaded, and what it refused. It does not change the machine, because the clock this core runs on is the emulated console's and does not depend on who reads the log. It is the first thing to turn on when a project will not start.
texts.slot.arcademedia.help: The game's own medium: the CD, DVD or hard disk that holds its data. It is read by the NAMCO board's disk controller (ATA/ATAPI) and not by the console's drive, because a COH-H board has no disc drive. The Media setting says which of the three it is, because the file itself does not. These are usually kept compressed as .chd. A plain .iso or .bin works too. This core works out how the sectors are laid out in the file (2048-byte data sectors, raw CD frames of 2352 or 2448 bytes, 2336-byte Mode 2, or raw DVD sectors of 2064 bytes) and does not rely on the extension. An incomplete file is refused with a message that says so, because a game that reads past the end of one fails much later and much less clearly.
texts.slot.bootelf.help: The program the board starts. On a real cabinet this is Sony's PSALM boot.bin, which is on the board. You do not have to copy it from a board. Proverb (github.com/PS2Homebrew-arcade/proverb, AFL-3.0) is an open alternative that starts the same games, and it comes with one boot.elf for each NAMCO part number. For example bin/NM00004/boot.elf is the one for Tekken 4. Either one works here. The one a project uses is part of the machine, so two projects with different boot programs are different machines and cannot share movies.
texts.slot.disc.help: What the machine runs. This is usually a DVD or CD image. It can be a plain .iso or .bin (with sectors of 2048 or 2352 bytes, with or without a .cue file beside it) or a compressed image (.chd, .cso, .zso, .gz). It can also be a PS2 EXECUTABLE (.elf), which is how homebrew and test programs are distributed. The tray then stays empty and the machine is given the program to run, exactly as it would run a disc's own boot file. The first four bytes of the file decide which it is, not its name, so an executable with any name still starts. A project with no file at all is a console showing its own browser, and that machine can be started too. But the New Project window asks for a file, because a movie is usually of a game. A game on several discs takes every disc, in order: the first is in the drive when the console is switched on, and the Next Disc, Previous Disc and Disc Swap controls change it when the game asks.
texts.slot.dongle.help: The game's security dongle. Without it an arcade game does not start at all. It is not a chip. It is a copy of the game's own COH-H10020 MEMORY CARD, 8,650,752 bytes long (8 MB plus error-correction data, the size PCSX2 keeps a card at), and it holds the boot software the board runs. Each game has its own, and another game's dongle starts nothing. The file is usually named after NAMCO's part number or after the label on the cartridge, with whatever extension the person who copied it chose. The name does not matter. The file is taken as it is and put in the board's card slot 1, where the cabinet has it. The file is never changed. The project and the movie record exactly which file it was. The boot software rewrites the dongle as it runs, and what a run wrote is exported as save data and is not written back into your copy.
texts.slot.savedata.help: What the machine starts with already saved. On a PlayStation 2 that is the memory cards and the console's own settings memory (NVRAM): memcard1.ps2, memcard2.ps2 and bios.nvm. A memory card from PCSX2 or anywhere else is taken under its own name (Mcd001.ps2, THPS.ps2): a card not named for a slot goes in slot 1, then slot 2, in the order listed here, and Export Save Data writes it back under the same name. On a NAMCO board it is sram.bin, the 32 KB of battery-backed settings memory on the board, which holds the coin settings and the options of the game's own test menu. These are the files that Emulator > Export Save Data... writes, given back under the same names. A run can then continue where another stopped, or start from a cabinet that somebody set up in the test menu. The files are never changed. The project and the movie record exactly which files they were, so a movie that starts from a saved game can be played back by anyone who has the same files. A file whose name nothing reads is refused when the project loads, and the message names it, so it is never silently ignored. Leave it empty and the machine starts with blank cards and a board that nobody has set up, which is a new console and a new cabinet.
